title: Multi-Region
subtitle: Geographic latency reduction, regional blast-radius survivability, and speed-of-light replication physics.
keyTakeaways: Multi-region architectures solve three distinct problems: surviving region-wide control-plane outages, reducing user round-trip latency via geographic proximity, and satisfying data sovereignty laws (GDPR).

Speed-of-light in fiber (~200 km/ms) imposes a hard physical floor: US-East to US-West is ~65ms RTT, and US to Europe is ~85-100ms RTT, making synchronous cross-region writes prohibitively slow for most interactive apps.
Control-plane dependencies (IAM, global DNS config updates, CI/CD) are the #1 cause of correlated multi-region outages; data planes must operate autonomously without calling regional control APIs.

sections.heading: Physics of WAN Latency & Data Replication Strategies
sections.body: While Multi-AZ protects against physical data center failures, an entire Cloud Region can go down due to a faulty regional software deployment, BGP routing leak, or regional control-plane service outage (e.g., AWS us-east-1 IAM/DynamoDB/Kinesis incidents). Spanning multiple regions introduces speed-of-light constraints.
bullets: Synchronous Cross-Region Quorum (Spanner / CockroachDB): Commits wait for a majority of regions (e.g., US-East, US-Central, US-West). Guarantees strict serializability and RPO = 0, but every write incurs 30-70ms minimum WAN RTT.

Asynchronous Cross-Region Replication (DynamoDB Global Tables / Aurora Global): Local region commits in <5ms and ships replication logs asynchronously over WAN (~1s replication lag). Fast writes, but risks stale reads or ~1s data loss on sudden regional crash.

Home-Region Pinning (Cellular Sharding): Partition users by geo-shard (e.g., EU users pinned to `eu-central-1`, US users to `us-east-1`) so 99% of reads and writes are strictly local, with async cross-region standby for DR.

sections.heading: Regional Isolation & Avoiding Correlated Global Outages
sections.body: Building a multi-region system that accidentally shares a single global bottleneck is worse than a single-region system because it doubles operational complexity without improving availability.
bullets: Staggered Ring Deployments: Never deploy a config change, schema migration, or binary update to all regions simultaneously. Roll out to Canary Region -> wait 4 hours -> Region 2 -> wait 24 hours -> Region 3.
Data Plane vs Control Plane Separation: During an outage, your regional traffic routing and failover must rely on static data-plane health checks, not control-plane mutation APIs.

Cache Warming on Regional Failover: If `us-east-1` fails and 100% of US traffic suddenly shifts to `us-west-2`, cold Redis caches in West will cause an instant database stampede unless caches are pre-warmed via cross-region replication streams.

tradeOffs.pros: Fast local read-after-write consistency (<10ms); avoids write conflicts; satisfies GDPR data residency.
tradeOffs.cons: Traveling users experience cross-region latency or require complex session/shard migration.
tradeOffs.bestFor: SaaS platforms, ride-sharing (Uber/Lyft), food delivery, and regional banking systems.

tradeOffs.pros: External consistency (linearizability) globally with zero conflict resolution code and RPO = 0.
tradeOffs.cons: Every write pays speed-of-light WAN latency (30-100ms+); high infrastructure and cross-region network cost.
tradeOffs.bestFor: Global financial ledgers, inventory reservation, and global IAM/configuration stores.

interviewTip: Quote real latency numbers in interviews: Intra-AZ is ~0.2ms, Cross-AZ is ~1-2ms, US East-to-West is ~65ms, and US-to-Europe is ~85ms. Use these numbers to prove why synchronous multi-region two-phase commit doesn't work for a <50ms SLA.
